newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish credit usage rises, seen supporting rates.
newsitem.headline: Polish credit usage rises, seen supporting rates.

text.p: Polish credit extension remained buoyant during the first quarter of the year and analysts said this might put the brake on any interest rate cuts for some time.

The National Bank of Poland (NBP) reported on Wednesday that credit extension grew 2.9 percent in March and 8.5 percent since the start of the year. Broad money supply grew 2.2 percent last month and 4.1 percent in the quarter.
"The March credit growth is unsettling...and it certainly signals that the NBP should enforce a very tight monetary policy," said Krzysztof Bledowski, head economist at WoodCommerz in Warsaw.
Analysts said credit, especially consumption credit for households, continued to grow despite increased lending rates.

They said the credit boom, which started in late 1996, was fuelled by fast growth of real wages along with easier access to credit financing, not readily available during the first years of transformation from communism because of high inflation.

"The average Pole...doesn't care how much he pays for credit, but lending rates are essential for firms and this is why personal credit is growing quicker than corporate lending," said Andrzej Burliga, analyst at Bank Zachondni SA.
During the first quarter personal credit grew 10 percent and corporate credit 8.3 percent.
Credit to non-financial institutions grew 44 percent amid falling interest rates in 1996, against a 30 percent rise in broad money supply. Lending to households soared 109 percent last year.
The fast rise of credit in March surprised many analysts, who expected credit growth to slow because of an increase in banks' obligatory reserves from the end of February.
In response to increased costs stemming from the reserve requirement rise many commercial banks pushed up credit rates.

Analysts, who earlier expected a third quarter reduction in official interest rates, set at 22 percent for the discount rate and 25 percent for Lombard, were now starting to look for the next move around the turn of the third and fourth quarters, if at all.
"Interest rates will remain at present levels, there is no reason to increase them and any cuts are not likely until at least the autumn," said Ewa Lipinska, analyst at PBK SA bank.

The central bank last week signalled interest rates might fall in the longer term when it refrained to increase yields of 182-day and 273-day NBP-bills after earlier lifting yields on its 91-day paper and its reverse repo drainages.
Interest rates were last trimmed in July 1996 when inflation was 20.4 percent year-on-year. Annual price growth stood at 17.3 percent in February. Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
